questions_asked: At a busy airport security checkpoint, which step makes the long line move slowest: showing documents to an officer, or going through the scanner with bags?

At a screening lane, which thing causes the biggest, most unpredictable delays: bags flagged for extra search, failed body scans needing a pat-down, or passengers taking long to pack and repack their belongings?
On a normal busy morning, what fraction of passengers' bags typically gets flagged for an extra manual search at a screening lane?
When a bag is flagged and pulled off the belt for manual search, does the whole screening lane keep moving, or do passengers back up behind it?
Do TSA agents usually open more open screening lanes as the morning peak arrives, or keep the same number open all morning?
At a US airport checkpoint, when several screening lanes have lines, do passengers typically join the shortest line, or stick with the one they first entered?
Do passengers typically give up their place in the security line to go back and re-pack or re-arrange their bags before scanning?
When a family or group with several bags arrives at a screening lane, do they typically go through one after another, or together as a group?
When a checkpoint line gets very long and slow, do passengers mainly complain and grumble, or do some actually leave and re-book a later flight?
At a busy airport, do passengers from different countries behave very differently in security lines, or is the difference in crowd behavior mostly within any one nationality?
expert_answers:
Going through the scanner with bags is the slower step.

Document/ID check is a short, fairly uniform transaction — typically on the order of 10–30 seconds per passenger, with little variability. The screening step is the bottleneck because it bundles several serial sub-tasks per passenger: unloading belongings into bins, the conveyor/X-ray pass, the walk-through metal detector or millimeter-wave scan, and re-collecting and re-dressing (shoes, belt, laptop, liquids) on the far side. That is commonly on the order of 1–3 minutes per passenger, and it is highly variable — flagged bags, pat-downs, and re-scans add large random delays.

So the scanner/baggage step both has the longer mean service time and the greater variance, which is what actually governs how fast the queue drains. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint timings, not a precise measured figure.

Bags flagged for extra search cause the biggest and most unpredictable delays.

A flagged bag triggers a manual bag check at Zone D: the bag is pulled off the belt, opened, and searched item by item, often with the passenger present. That is typically on the order of 1–5 minutes per event, and it is highly variable — it depends on what was flagged, whether the passenger is cooperative, and whether a supervisor is needed. It also blocks the lane while it happens.

Failed body scans needing a pat-down are also disruptive but usually shorter and more bounded — commonly 30 seconds to 2 minutes, and often resolved by a re-scan.

Passengers packing/repacking belongings is the most predictable of the three: it adds time to every passenger, but it is routine and roughly similar each time, so it raises the mean without adding much variance.

This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint behavior, not a measured figure.

Roughly 5–15% of bags get flagged for extra manual search on a normal busy morning. In practice it is often toward the lower end of that range — commonly cited as on the order of 5–10% — with the rate rising during peak periods or when new equipment/procedures are in place. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint behavior, not a precise measured figure.

The whole lane does not keep moving — passengers back up behind it.

A flagged bag is pulled off the belt at the far end and searched at Zone D, usually with the passenger held there. That passenger cannot clear the lane and collect their belongings until the search finishes, so they occupy the exit/reclaim area. Meanwhile the belt and the body scanner keep feeding the next passengers into that same lane, and those passengers also cannot exit past the stopped one. The result is a queue that grows behind the flagged bag for the duration of the search.

The one qualification: the lane's upstream sub-steps (ID check, bin loading, X-ray, body scan) can physically continue for a short while, because there is buffer space on the belt and in the queue. So it is not an instant full stop — it is a blockage that propagates backward and stalls the lane if the search runs long. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint behavior, not a measured figure.

More lanes are opened as the morning peak arrives — staffing is adjusted to demand, not held constant.

Checkpoint lane counts are set by a staffing plan tied to forecast passenger volume, and the morning peak is the main driver. Typically a fraction of lanes run overnight/early, then additional lanes are opened in the hour or two before the peak and closed again after it passes. The TSA's post-2016 response to long lines was explicitly to add staffing and open more lanes at congested airports during peak periods.

Two qualifications that matter for modeling: lane openings are lumpy and lagged — they happen in discrete steps when staff arrive, not smoothly with the arrival curve — and the Pre-Check-to-regular lane ratio (often about 1:3) is a policy choice that may not track the actual 45% Pre-Check share. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint practice, not a measured figure.

Passengers typically join the shortest line, not the one they first entered.

At a US checkpoint, Zone B is a pooled queue that feeds whichever screening lanes are open; passengers are directed to the next available lane rather than choosing one and staying. Where passengers do self-select, they generally pick the visibly shortest queue — this is the common "jockeying" behavior in multi-server queues.

Two qualifications that matter for modeling: passengers cannot freely switch once they are committed to a lane (bins loaded, belongings on the belt), so any switching happens only at the point of lane assignment; and because the lanes are largely fed by a single pooled queue, the practical behavior is closer to "next available server" than to independent shortest-line choice. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint practice, not a measured figure.

No — passengers essentially never give up their place in line to go back and re-pack.

Once a passenger is in the queue, they hold their spot; leaving means losing it and rejoining at the back, which no one does voluntarily. Re-packing and re-arranging happens in place, at the front of the line or at the bin-loading area, while the passenger stays in position. This is exactly why slow packers block the lane rather than stepping aside.

The one qualification: a passenger may be pulled out of line by an officer (e.g., for a secondary check), but that is directed, not voluntary. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint behavior, not a measured figure.

Together as a group, not one after another.

A family or group arriving at a screening lane typically stays together through the process. They load their bins onto the belt consecutively, and the individuals pass through the metal detector or millimeter-wave scanner back-to-back, then wait for each other on the far side to re-collect belongings and re-dress before moving on. The group does not split up to be served as independent units.

Two qualifications that matter for modeling: the group occupies the lane as a block, so its service time is roughly the sum of its members' times plus the shared packing/reclaim overhead — this raises the effective service time and adds variance at that lane; and because members wait for each other at the exit, a slow member (or one pulled for a pat-down) holds the whole group in the reclaim area, which can stall the lane behind them. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint behavior, not a measured figure.

Mostly they stay and grumble; only a small minority actually leave and re-book.

Passengers in a security line are usually already committed — they have a flight to catch, checked bags, and no easy way to re-book without cost or lost time. So the dominant response is complaint and frustration, not exit. Leaving the line means missing the flight, and re-booking is expensive and often impractical on the spot.

The exceptions are a small fraction: passengers with very long connection buffers, those on flexible/refundable tickets, or those who judge they will clearly miss the flight anyway. Those may abandon the line and re-book.

For modeling, the practical implication is that the queue is essentially closed — abandonment is negligible, so the line keeps growing rather than self-regulating through passenger exit. This is an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

Mostly within any one nationality — the between-country differences are real but smaller than the spread inside a single nationality.

The behaviors that matter at a checkpoint (how fast someone packs and repacks, how much personal space they leave, whether they crowd forward or hold back, how readily they follow officer instructions) vary widely among individuals of the same nationality. Age, familiarity with flying, group size, and whether they are Pre-Check or regular travelers often dominate over national origin.

National/cultural norms do shift the average — e.g., a stronger personal-space norm makes a queue looser and slower to close up, while an efficiency-first norm makes people fill gaps faster — but these are modest shifts in the mean, not a different regime. For a sensitivity analysis, treat nationality as a small adjustment to the mean and variance of service/queue behavior, not as a separate behavioral class.

This is an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.
